It's complicated. Primarily because of two things. Where the ash will go is hugely dependent upon wind conditions and time of year. The raining ash at least. The second thing is that there have been multiple eruptions from Yellowstone in the past. Some smaller, and some larger. The largest one rained ash on the Texas-Mexico border. The smallest only made it to like upper Kansas. Huge difference.

Here is a map based on the assumption that the eruption would be 75-85% as large as the one that covered 70% of the US in ash: http://www.geoengineeringwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/file/killzone-hotash.jpg

People will be immediately dead in the red, shortly dead in the brown, and it will be very hard to live in the yellow areas.

The Kill Zone is a combo of the super heated wall of ash and the sound. A compressed wave of air is very deadly to normal life. Here's a GIF of a small eruption in Papua New Guinea: http://a2.files.blazepress.com/image/upload/MTI4OTkzNDkxMTExMDIzODkw.gif

Mt. Saint Hellens was several times larger than that, and Yellowstone would be thousands of times larger. Here's a comparison map: http://www.cuttingedge.org/Yellowstone_SuperVolcano.jpg

And here's the various landfalls of Yellowstone's past eruptions to get a sense of where it's boundaries are: http://s2.djyimg.com/n3/eet-content/uploads/2014/07/29/yellowstone-eruption-map-new-636x450.jpg

Here are some more comparisons between various large eruptions we have record of, compared to Yellowstone: https://www.nps.gov/yell/learn/nature/images/caldera_eruptions2_1.jpg

Krakatoa made the loudest sound we've heard, which reverberated throughout the globe 7 times before dissipating. It would be anywhere from 15 to 150 times smaller than a Yellowstone potential eruption. http://volcano.oregonstate.edu/historical-eruption-sounds

Here's a page listing what could be expected of people living within range of Yellowstone after an eruption: https://heavenawaits.wordpress.com/yellowstone-park-volcano/
